decisions.rationale: Artifact drill-through is a nearby command consumer, but it does not establish the same OpenArtifact resolution authority, precedence, or attempt-link lifecycle.
The comparator routes artifact consumers but does not own approval-scoped visibility, revocation propagation, or already-open artifact behavior.
Terminal acceptance and Chat terminal projection are plausible neighboring surfaces, but preview, browser, terminal, and tab section recovery is a different documentation and ownership lifecycle.

Project switching, background worktree routing, and workspace identity consume project context, but each has a distinct authority and transition lifecycle from shared cross-surface context propagation.
Git conflict transitions are a plausible neighbor, but the anchor governs File Manager operation-conflict sessions rather than the Git conflict state machine.

The comparators define Source Control commands, compare identity, and conflict transitions; the anchor instead concerns cross-owner diff and review routing and therefore is not coextensive with any one lifecycle.
Host-aware editor projections are adjacent, but remote search/LSP restoration has a different producer and recovery state machine from diagnostic marker revision and precedence projection.
PF-0042 is the same Source Control compare-target identity and stale-target lifecycle, while provider-backed remote review adds a separate permission, pagination, and force-push lifecycle.
Artifact routing and worktree-aware file pivots share file identity concerns, but neither owns Assistant composer-chip insertion, access recheck, removal, and send-time resolution.

Destructive Source Control, Git conflict transitions, and index-hunk mutations are close consumers, but the anchor combines policy-controlled hunk and conflict launch routing rather than any one comparator's execution lifecycle.
Artifact drill-through and worktree-aware file identity are adjacent routing inputs, but neither is the narrow OpenFile payload, coordinate, containment, and rejection contract.
These catalog families expose the named shell consumers and wrappers, but the anchor is PlanUnit dependency governance rather than their runtime command authority or lifecycle.
Search-tool separation and Search-owner actions are nearby, but local tree filtering has a distinct immediate UI consumer and no shared search-index mutation lifecycle.
Route/open wrappers and artifact navigation consume normalized references, but the anchor owns the discriminator and legacy-ID normalization boundary, not those consumer command lifecycles.

The comparators cover individual file mutations, worktree file identity, and root projection; the anchor is the broader Composer/File Manager/Editor surface contract and therefore has a different scope and consumer promise.
No comparator represents canonical formatter ownership under the formatter execution and evidence authority.
File-mutation receipt identity is a plausible trigger input, but formatter dispatch events have a separate producer, ordering, replay, and idempotency lifecycle.
No comparator covers the formatter-to-Plugins_System/FileSafe authorization handoff or its denial and enforcement contract.
No comparator shares the sequential formatter-chain authority, per-file serialization, revision, and concurrent-edit lifecycle.
No comparator addresses the formatter-specific whitespace evidence contradiction or the same event-emission rule.
General rollback features do not share the formatter non-zero-exit preservation, chain continuation, backup, and atomic restore lifecycle.
No comparator owns the built-in formatter catalog or executable-detection cache and freshness lifecycle.

Git binary execution integrity and test-child cancellation are security-adjacent subprocess contracts, but they use different command authorities, consumers, and termination state machines from formatter execution.
File mutations and worktree-aware identity share path-safety inputs, but `$FILE` substitution is governed by formatter dispatch and FileSafe revalidation rather than those operation lifecycles.
No comparator represents custom formatter identity, scope collisions, provenance, enablement, and first-run trust states.
No comparator shares the global/project formatter configuration merge, tombstone, precedence, and invalid-layer recovery lifecycle.
No comparator is the Formatter Settings GUI or its persistence, recovery, secret, provenance, and runnable-state contract.
No comparator shares the formatter settings interaction-mode accessibility, localization, and active-configuration disclosure promise.
No comparator is the OpenCode formatter-baseline lineage or its detection, placeholder, and custom-formatter compatibility boundary.
No comparator represents the Puppet Master-specific formatter runtime deltas across Rust dispatch, resolution, evidence, and HTE enforcement.

Structured terminal events and file-mutation receipt identity are neighboring evidence systems, but formatter events have distinct schema ownership, correlation, hashing, and stderr-redaction semantics.
No comparator concerns the retired formatter bridge and its lineage-only authority boundary.
No comparator represents formatter ordering ownership or the orphaned duplicate-formatter oracle.
GitHub auth commands and provider review consume the locked credential/API boundary, but neither owns the full SSOT split across credentials, local Git, remote SSH, UICommand, and imported lineage.
These comparators instantiate named consumers, but the anchor is the cross-owner reconciliation boundary spanning auth, runtime, storage, FileSafe, routing, approval, and search authorities.

The command catalog and operational-panel family are close consumers, but the anchor owns the GitHub Integration surface separation and accessible accordion promise rather than their command or shared-recovery lifecycles.
Compare-target safety and remote review are adjacent, but the anchor additionally binds requested and effective GitHub account identity under an attribution lifecycle absent from both comparators.
Git conflict transitions also use safe points and rollback, but the anchor's focus-preserving restore/retry confirmation and declined no-change outcome are a distinct user-visible lifecycle.
Actions commands, namespace migration, and pin persistence are direct neighbors; none is coextensive with the combined Actions IA, pinned-workflow lifecycle, and same-branch replay feature.
Stale compare and remote permission states can gate actions, but GitHub Actions live-admin readiness and mutation denial have a distinct authority and capability state machine.
No comparator owns GitHub run correlation or impact-map heuristics, thresholds, tie-breaks, retention, and false-result oracles.
GitHub Actions command coverage and namespace rules are adjacent, but log triage and workflow preview/apply have distinct payload, concurrency, partial-write, retry, and rollback lifecycles.

Deferred-run terminality and worktree validity expose neighboring blocked states, but they use different authorities and recovery state machines from the GitHub attention, auth, policy, and governance taxonomy.

Worktree confirmation, destructive recovery, ownership, and filter state are plausible component features, but none matches the combined Source Control worktree topology UI, lifecycle, accessibility, and concurrent-confirmation contract.
Runtime wrappers, stable consumer routing, and worktree commands instantiate seams named by the anchor, but each retains its own authority and lifecycle.
Bundle approval lineage is approval-adjacent, but graph-patch application uses different identities, generations, concurrency, partial-apply rollback, and cancellation authority.

Remote Git cache trust, crash-atomic publication, and host-aware recovery are close storage neighbors, but remote path guards and reconnect handling govern a separate GitHub remote-execution security lifecycle.

Remote-cache trust and publication may supply verification anchors, but in-flight remote tool mutation atomicity and stale-anchor handling have a distinct execution authority and transaction lifecycle.
Provider review and remote-repository creation consume authenticated account state, but neither owns requested/effective-account snapshot freshness, check-to-use races, and receipt retention.
No comparator is the retired GitHub bridge or shares its lineage-only non-ownership lifecycle.

Remote review, repository creation, and PR-panel handoff are plausible consumers, but optional promotion and discovery spans request deduplication, push/PR/check partial outcomes, attachment rollback, and cross-owner receipt reconciliation.
No comparator represents GitHub update-currentness and release-tag verification with its endpoint, version ordering, cache, offline, concurrency, and receipt lifecycle.

Worktree removal, allocation cleanup, thread-delete cleanup, and parallel worktree recovery are close cleanup consumers, but the anchor owns the workspace-scoped git-clean allow/protect policy and its own safety boundary.

Canonical thread binding, worktree commands, binding storage, and creation UI are plausible realizations, but the concept-only dropdown actions lack enough authority and lifecycle identity to prove they are the same feature.

Search command workflow and Search-panel owner routing are adjacent, but scope selection, result-group focus, and result opening are read-navigation wiring with a different mutation and stale-snapshot lifecycle.
Search snapshot validation is a strong neighbor, but the anchor governs opening a possibly moved, deleted, or out-of-range result, while PF-0033 governs search mutation and bulk-replace recovery.
PF-0033 is the same Search-owner replace and traversal command workflow with preserved result snapshots; PF-0040 is the broader stable-owner routing family rather than the mutation lifecycle itself.
Production worktree commands and Source Control ownership are the intended neighboring authorities, but non-authoritative mock lineage is not itself their product execution lifecycle.

The comparators cover command families and destructive/index execution semantics, but the anchor combines diff-open alias normalization with unstage and discard wiring identities, so no single comparator is the same full feature.

PF-0050 explicitly covers the same discard-hunk command and its missing confirmation, stale-target, recovery, and propagation contract; broader destructive-command and conflict-transition families remain related but distinct.
No comparator covers the accessible-name failure for symbol-only Git hunk controls under the same user-visible command promise.

Worktree command wiring, branch identity, and Source Control branch safety are intended neighbors, but concept-only branch/stash fixtures do not establish the same authority, command set, or lifecycle.

Worktree wiring, destructive recovery, Source Control merge safety, and merge locking are component lifecycles; the anchor combines merge, validation, and worktree settings controls without a canonical shared authority.

Lane capacity, DAG scheduling, and parallel-admission caps are plausible implementations, but anonymous concept settings do not identify their scheduler authority, units, admission lifecycle, or failure state machine.
Worktree command wiring and Source Control branch/merge ownership are close authorities, but the unbound Git Operations GUI concept lacks enough command and lifecycle identity to merge.
PF-0063 is the same Source Control-owned branch, merge, rebase, guard, and recovery lifecycle; dialog guard details and merge-lock atomicity are narrower related subfeatures.

Clipboard/paste/save-copy and create/delete are adjacent File Manager mutation families, but the anchor specifically governs copy/move overwrite conflict resolution and keep-both semantics, a distinct command and recovery lifecycle.
Completion and Source Control receipts are constituent receipt families, but packaging all plans-to-code receipt families is a separate artifact authority and validation lifecycle.
No comparator represents Quickstart derived-output authority, limit determinism, or validation command grammar.
Shell-failure and write-thrash counters are neighboring run guards, but RM-018 uses an exact repeated tool-call/error fingerprint and a distinct termination trigger and reset lifecycle.

Terminal layering, parser replay, and lifecycle events are close consumers of PTY bytes, but framing, delivery, reconnect, backpressure, corruption, and excerpt authorization form a distinct transport contract.
